query: For multi-component concentrated alloys, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs their strength and deformation or failure behavior, and why? Specify a controlled comparison that would reveal the governing cause, the observations predicted relative to a baseline, the conditions over which the hypothesis should hold, the prior evidence supporting it, and an outcome that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In single‐phase, multi‐component concentrated alloys, local chemical short‐range ordering (SRO) induces spatial fluctuations in shear‐fault energy that act as nanoscale pinning zones for dislocations, thereby increasing the activation barrier for dislocation glide. This results in higher yield strength and altered strain hardening, which governs the overall deformation and failure behavior, especially at high temperatures by means of the chemical short‐range order effect.
generation.material_initial_state: A fully solid‐solution high-entropy alloy (e.g., an FCC NiCoCr or CoCrFeNi alloy) produced via conventional casting/annealing with minimal SRO.
generation.intervention: Apply controlled thermo-mechanical treatments (e.g., targeted annealing or controlled deformation) to promote the development of local chemical SRO without changing overall composition, versus a reference treatment (e.g., rapid quenching or severe plastic deformation) that minimizes SRO.
generation.conditions: Tests should be conducted at room temperature and at elevated temperatures relevant to high-temperature applications (for example, at a high temperature) on single-phase HEAs or concentrated alloys with similar lattice structures. The alloy must remain single-phase so that dislocation glide (rather than twinning or phase transformation) is the dominant mechanism.
generation.structural_mediator: The evolution of local SRO creates regions of variable stacking/shear-fault energy (i.e. hard atomic motifs) that locally impede dislocation motions.
generation.mechanism: The increased local ordering raises the energy barriers for dislocation motion by creating a rugged energy landscape with heterogeneous shear-fault energies. In turn, dislocations are forced to overcome higher activation energies and often follow more tortuous pathways, which enhances yield strength and adjusts work hardening behavior. Conversely, alloys processed to minimize SRO have more uniform fault energies, lower activation barriers, and consequently lower strength. This process is directly controlled by the chemical short‐range order effect.
generation.predicted_outcome: Samples processed to enhance SRO will display a noticeably higher yield strength (and likely an elevated work hardening rate) along with dislocation patterns indicative of pinning by hard atomic regions compared to baseline samples with minimized SRO. This difference should be observable at both room and elevated temperatures, although quantitative differences may depend on the specific alloy system and processing parameters.
generation.baseline: High-entropy alloy samples processed via methods (e.g., severe plastic deformation or rapid quenching) that yield a near-random atomic distribution (minimal SRO), exhibiting lower yield strength and more homogeneous dislocation glide.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis is expected to hold for single-phase concentrated alloys (HEAs or medium-entropy alloys) where dislocation-mediated plasticity predominates. It might not apply or may need modification for alloys dominated by phase transformation, extensive twinning, or where multiphase microstructures strongly influence behavior.
generation.uncertainty: The precise magnitude of strength enhancement attributable solely to SRO-induced shear-fault energy fluctuations is uncertain, as it may interplay with other factors (e.g., lattice distortion effects). Systematic variation in composition and processing may be required to isolate SRO contributions.

falsification_experiment.design: Fabricate two sets of high-entropy alloy samples with identical compositions. Process one set using a thermal treatment designed to promote SRO (e.g., annealing at a temperature that favours local ordering) and process the other set using rapid quenching or intensive deformation to suppress SRO. Characterize the degree of local ordering by techniques such as atom probe tomography or synchrotron diffraction. Subject both sets to identical tensile tests at room and elevated temperatures.
measurements: Quantitative evaluation of yield strength and work hardening rate via mechanical testing
Microstructural and dislocation analysis via TEM or high-resolution microscopy to reveal differences in dislocation pinning and slip paths
Direct or indirect characterization of SRO (e.g., via APT, X-ray/neutron diffraction)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the samples with enhanced SRO do not exhibit a statistically significant increase in yield strength, altered strain hardening behavior, or dislocation patterns indicative of increased pinning relative to the low-SRO baseline samples, then the hypothesis that SRO-induced shear-fault energy fluctuations govern the mechanical behavior will be rejected.

cited_evidence.text: SignificanceComplex concentrated alloys (CCAs) with multi elements in equiatomic ratios are exotic alloys but what governs their strength is currently not clearly understood. This work has proven the prime origin of strength in CCAs as arising from the fluctuations (not the averaged value) of the shear-fault energy, which is an important feature of CCAs unrecognized beforehand. Through identification of the local hard atomic motifs far beyond the traditional concept of the globally averaged short-range ordering parameters, this work has unfolded the physical basis of strength in CCAs and provides important clues for designing high-strength CCAs by focusing on the alloy composition to produce large fault-energy fluctuations. Local chemical short-range ordering (SRO) and spatial fluctuations of planar fault energy are important features of multi-element and metastable complex concentrated alloys (CCAs). Arising from them, dislocations in such alloys are distinctively wavy in both static and migrating conditions; yet, such effects on strength have remained unknown. High-entropy and medium-entropy alloys are presumed to have a configurational entropy as high as that of an ideally mixed solid solution (SS) of multiple elements in near-equal proportions. However, enthalpic interactions inevitably render such chemically disordered SSs rare and metastable, except at very high temperatures. Here we highlight the wide variety of local chemical ordering (LCO) that sets these concentrated SSs apart from traditional solvent-solute ones. Using atomistic simulations, we reveal that the LCO of the multi-principal-element NiCoCr SS changes with alloy processing conditions, producing a wide range of generalized planar fault energies. We show that the LCO heightens the ruggedness of the energy landscape and raises activation barriers governing dislocation activities. This influences the selection of dislocation pathways in slip, faulting, and twinning, and increases the lattice friction to dislocation motion via a nanoscale segment detrapping mechanism. In contrast, severe plastic deformation reduces the LCO towards random SS. Multi-principal-element alloys have been assumed to have the configurational entropy of an ideal solution. cited_evidence.kind: web:Strategy to design HEAs with large strength and ductility via SRO
cited_evidence.text: We performed iterative MC and MD simulations to examine the evolution of SRO in the CoCuFeNiPd HEA and MD simulations to investigate the effect of SRO on mechanical behavior. During the formation of SRO, some small regions transform to BCC-preferred structures (BCC is more stable than FCC), while others become very strongly FCC-preferred structures (FCC is much more stable than BCC). The resulting structure is a pseudo-composite microstructure consisting of very stable FCC-preferred (FCCP) regions and BCC-preferred (BCCP) regions in a matrix of marginal stability. Tensile-deformation simulations indicate that the ultimate strength and ductility of the HEA are both enhanced by the development of the SRO. The origin of these enhancements can be traced to the SRO-induced pseudo-composite microstructure that forms; this consists of both FCCP hardening domains and BCCP toughening domains in a matrix of marginal phase stability. We propose a strategy for simultaneously achieving excellent strength and ductility via SRO in HEAs.
